paper_b.title: Problems and Results on 3-Chromatic Hypergraphs and Some Related Questions

metadata.description: Both papers wield the probabilistic method to prove existence of combinatorial colorings, but they target different problems and deploy distinct probabilistic machinery. Spencer (1985) settles Erdos's set-discrepancy question via a partial-coloring argument that combines Hoeffding tail bounds, entropy counting, pigeonhole and Kleitman's isodiametric inequality. Erdos-Lovasz (1975) introduce the Local Lemma and apply it to chromatic-number problems on uniform hypergraphs (and to a lattice-point translate-coloring problem of Strauss). Aside from the shared probabilistic-method scaffolding and the recurring use of subgaussian / CLT-style tail bounds, the technical machineries are largely disjoint, so node-level matches are sparse and analogical rather than exact.

matches.explanation: Spencer's subgaussian Rademacher-sum tail bound (Hoeffding/Chernoff) is the workhorse tail estimate for the partial-coloring lemma. Erdos-Lovasz's proof of the Strauss-translate Theorem 4 (PP346.5) appeals to a CLT-derived tail probability $(1-\delta)^r$ on each translate failing to receive a color in the right proportion. Both invoke the same family of subgaussian / CLT tail behaviour for sums of independent Bernoulli/Rademacher variables, but in different roles: Spencer uses it to bound how often a random sign-vector overshoots $\lambda\sqrt{n}$, while Erdos-Lovasz use it to bound monochromatic / unbalanced events in random colorings before applying the local lemma.

Both are the namesake existence lemmas of the two papers, used to power all downstream existence theorems via the probabilistic method. Spencer's Lemma 4 produces a three-valued $\{-1,0,+1\}$ partial coloring with few zeros and small linear forms via a probabilistic-counting + pigeonhole + Kleitman extraction. Erdos-Lovasz's symmetric Local Lemma asserts $P(\bigcap \overline{A_i}) > 0$ when each event is sparsely dependent. Conceptually they fill the same slot - 'the probabilistic existence engine of this paper' - but the techniques are quite different (entropy/compactness vs. dependency-graph induction). Type compatibility (lemma-lemma) and shared role justify analogous; statements/proofs differ enough to rule out exact.

Spencer's main existence theorems (linear forms / set discrepancy / arbitrary-finite-set discrepancy) and Erdos-Lovasz's Theorem 4 (Strauss translate-coloring) all assert the existence of a coloring of an integer / vertex set making each member of a family of subsets balanced or non-monochromatic. Spencer phrases it as discrepancy bounded by $K\sqrt{n}$; Erdos-Lovasz phrase it as each translate $S+a$ containing at least $(1-\epsilon)r/k$ points of every color. Both target balanced colorings of a structured family of sets, with the bound depending on the family's size. The cluster A-side captures Spencer's three closely-linked main theorems (linear forms, $n$-set discrepancy, arbitrary finite sets) since they are essentially one result; the B-side is Erdos-Lovasz's only theorem of comparably 'discrepancy-flavored' content.

Both proofs are the technical heart of their respective papers. Spencer's proof of Lemma 4 chains a probabilistic lower bound on $|T^{-1}(B)|$, an entropy upper bound on $|B|$, pigeonhole, and Kleitman's isodiametric inequality. The Erdos-Lovasz proof of the local lemma is an inductive bound on conditional probabilities $P(A_1 \mid \bigcap_{j>1}\overline{A_j}) \le 1/(2d)$. The two proofs share only the high-level template 'random object satisfies all constraints with positive probability' but differ in every concrete step; the parent-level analogous match is recorded here, and per the v2 step-block rule we do not emit per-step matches between PSP345.* and PSP346.LLL.* (their inner step DAGs are not meaningfully aligned).

Binary entropy function $H(\alpha)$ is Spencer's external import (used in entropy counting of $|B|$); it has no counterpart in Erdos-Lovasz, whose probabilistic estimates rely on the dependency graph rather than entropy. Skipping per the origin/external rule would also be appropriate, but DP345.4 is referenced by paper-original lemmas and is informative, so we record it as none.

Discrepancy of a set under a two-coloring is Spencer's central object; Erdos-Lovasz are concerned with chromatic numbers of hypergraphs and translate-balanced colorings, not with discrepancy in this exact sense. There is no comparable definition in paper346.
Rudin-Shapiro polynomial is a Spencer-specific application (Theorem 11, Corollary 13) with no Erdos-Lovasz analogue.
Hamming diameter of subsets of $\{-1,+1\}^r$ is needed for Spencer's Kleitman-extraction step; Erdos-Lovasz never use this notion.
Spencer's $r$-variable generalization of Lemma 4 is internal scaffolding for iterating to Theorem 7; no analogue in paper346.
Theorem 7 (linear forms with $r \le n$ variables and the $\sqrt{\ln(2n/r)}$ factor) is Spencer-specific; no counterpart in Erdos-Lovasz.
Iteration of Lemma 6 to prove Theorem 7 is internal to Spencer's argument; no analogue in paper346.
Corollary 8 (rounding fractional initial values to $\{0,1\}$ while preserving linear forms) is Spencer-specific.
Theorem 9 (reduction to $n$ variables via underdetermined linear systems) is Spencer-specific.
Theorem 10 (linear forms with $r > n$ variables) is Spencer-specific.
Existence of Rudin-Shapiro polynomials (Theorem 11) is Spencer-specific.
Theorem 12 (exponentially many low-discrepancy assignments) is Spencer-specific.
Corollary 13 (many Rudin-Shapiro polynomials) is Spencer-specific.
Theorem 14 (improved Beck-Spencer $K\sqrt{i}$ bound on the $i$th form) is Spencer-specific.
Lemma 15 (step lemma for Theorem 14, with index-dependent bounds) is Spencer-specific.
Lemma 17 (elementary log-concavity bound used in entropy estimates) is Spencer-specific.
Theorem 16 (three-valued Komlos signing with bounded $L^\infty$ norm) is Spencer-specific.
Corollary 18 ($K\ln n$ bound for the Komlos signing problem) is Spencer-specific.
Theorem 19 (matching $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ lower bound via Hadamard matrix) is Spencer-specific.
Two proofs of the Hadamard / counting lower bound (Theorem 19) are Spencer-specific.
Lemma 20 (CLT-based sharpening of Lemma 6) is Spencer-specific.

Hypergraph terminology (edges, points, degree, $r$-uniform) is the foundation of Erdos-Lovasz; Spencer works with linear forms over $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and discrepancy of subsets, not with the language of $r$-uniform hypergraphs.
Simple hypergraph and clique definitions have no Spencer counterpart.
Chromatic number of a hypergraph: Spencer's discrepancy is morally about $2$-colorings but the chromatic-number invariant itself is not used.
Extremal counting functions $m_k(r), m_k^*(r), n_k^*(r)$ are Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Line-graph of a hypergraph is needed by Erdos-Lovasz to set up the local-lemma dependency graph; Spencer never uses line-graphs.
Hypergraph circuit / girth is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Clique-extremal functions $m^{**}(r), M(r), N(r)$ are Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
$q(r)$ (covering threshold for cliques) is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Edge-intersection-size set $\Delta(H)$ is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Asymptotic order of $n_k^*$ and $m_k^*$ has no Spencer counterpart.

Probabilistic existence of high-girth high-chromatic uniform hypergraphs (Theorem 1') is Erdos-Lovasz-specific; the construction is greedy/probabilistic but unrelated to Spencer's partial-coloring lemma.
Greedy edge-by-edge construction proving Theorem 1' is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
High-degree edge in chromatic-rich uniform hypergraphs (Theorem 2) is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Proof of Theorem 2 via the local lemma is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Degree-based colorability corollary is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Vertex-count lower bound for simple chromatic-rich uniform hypergraphs is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Rainbow-coloring theorem under bounded edge intersection is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Proof of Theorem 3 via the local lemma is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Many-high-degree-vertices theorem (Theorem 5) is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Delete-and-apply-Theorem-2 proof of Theorem 5 is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Covering lower bound for simple chromatic-rich is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Matching-size lower bound is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Edge lower bound for simple chromatic-rich is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Iterated Fano-plane construction of small $3$-chromatic cliques is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Proof of Theorem 6 via iterated Fano construction is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Bounds on $M(r)$ are Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Proof of Theorem 7 (bounds on $M(r)$) is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Bounds on $N(r)$ via Lubell-style permutation count are Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Proof of Theorem 8 (Lubell-style permutation argument) is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Lubell-style sharpening of Calczynska-Karlowicz is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Erdos-Lovasz-Shelah common-intersection bound ($r/\log r$) is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
$|\Delta(H)| \geq 3$ for large $r$ (Theorem 9) is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Proof of Theorem 9 (uses Deza's sunflower theorem) is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Bounds on $q(r)$ (Theorem 10) are Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Greedy lower bound + random projective lines upper bound proof for $q(r)$ is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Conjecture on $f(r) \to \infty$ for nonuniform $3$-chromatic hypergraphs is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Weakened-(1)-for-simple-hypergraphs conjecture is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Open problem on $\lim m^{**}(r)^{1/r} > 2$ is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Open problem on $\max \Delta(H) \geq r - O(1)$ is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Open problem on $|\Delta(H)| \to \infty$ is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
Open problem on $q(r) \le c \cdot r$ is Erdos-Lovasz-specific.
